a: Keep watch
t: Watch your feet, and the verse numbers
p: A Hebrew idiom for careful conduct. In Hebrew Bibles this verse is 4:17, so chapter 5 runs one verse behind.
b: To "keep watch over your feet" means to watch how you walk: think about where you are going and how you behave there (compare Proverbs 4:26–27). The written Hebrew text (Ketiv) has "your feet"; the Masoretes' reading tradition (Qere) has the singular "your foot", as the KJV does (see the variant). Verse numbers: this site, like most English Bibles, follows the KJV numbering. Hebrew Bibles, and the Greek, end chapter 4 with this verse (4:17) and number the rest of chapter 5 one lower, so English 5:2–20 is Hebrew 5:1–19. The word-by-word Hebrew and the literal lines used to make this translation are keyed to the English numbers. A reader checking a Jewish translation or commentary such as Rashi on "5:5" should look here at 5:6.

a: the house of God
p: The only place where Qohelet speaks of worship: the Temple in Jerusalem, rebuilt after the exile.
b: "The house of God" (bet ha'elohim) is the Temple, as in Ezra 5:2 and Nehemiah 13:11, the usual name for it in the books written after the exile. If Qohelet wrote in the Persian or early Greek period, as most scholars think, this was the Second Temple, rebuilt about 516 BC, with its priests, sacrifices, vows and prayers. Qohelet is not against worship: 5:1–7 is a short piece of advice on how to behave there. What he warns against is careless religion: hurried words, rash promises and sacrifices offered as if God could be managed. He uses the general word Elohim, "God", throughout the book and never the name YHWH.

a: Coming close to listen
p: Qohelet echoes the prophets and Proverbs: God wants an obedient ear more than an offering.
b: In Hebrew "listen" (shama') also means "obey". Samuel told Saul, "Look: listening is better than sacrifice" (1 Samuel 15:22), and Proverbs says the sacrifice of the wicked is abhorrent to the LORD (Proverbs 15:8; compare Proverbs 21:3, 27). Hosea and Amos say the same in other words (Hosea 6:6; Amos 5:21–24). Qohelet's twist is typical: the fool is not wicked so much as careless, someone who thinks an offering can stand in for attention. The Greek and the Syriac divide the line differently, "your sacrifice is better than the gift of fools" (see the variant).
r: 1 Samuel 15:22; Proverbs 15:8; Proverbs 21:3; Proverbs 21:27; Hosea 6:6; Amos 5:21–24; Psalm 40:6

a: for they do not know it when they do evil
p: The Hebrew is short and odd: 'they do not know to do evil'. Three readings are possible.
b: Word for word the clause says "for they do not know to do evil". (1) The Plain and most translations take it to mean that fools do wrong without noticing it; the KJV reads it this way too, "they consider not that they do evil". (2) Some read it with irony, supplying a word: "they know nothing except doing evil". (3) Others take "to do" as the object of knowing: fools do not know how to act, so they end up doing harm. The Targum expands the line in its own direction: fools bring sacrifices for their sins without leaving off their evil works, "for they know not whether they do good or evil" (Ginsburg's English). All the readings agree on the point: careless worship is not neutral.
orig: כִּי־אֵינָם יוֹדְעִים לַעֲשׂוֹת רָע (ki 'enam yod'im la'asot ra')

a: God is in the heavens, and you are on the earth
t: God in the heavens, you on the earth
p: The reason for few words is distance: God is God and you are not.
b: The contrast is not that God is far away and does not care, but that a human being has no standing to lecture God or bargain with him. Psalm 115:3 says: "Our God is in the heavens; / everything he wants, he does." Jesus warns against babbling in prayer as if many words would win a hearing (Matthew 6:7–8), and James tells believers to be quick to listen and slow to speak (James 1:19). Jewish teachers used this verse to argue for short, careful prayers (Talmud, Berakhot 61a). The Targum adds that God sits on the throne of glory and "rules over all the world".

a: For dreams come with too many tasks
p: A proverb: as a crowded day produces crowded dreams, a fool's mouth produces too many words.
b: The word for "tasks" ('inyan) is the one Qohelet uses for the "evil task" God gave human beings (1:13; 2:23; 3:10; 4:8). Here it means work and worry that fill the mind. The saying is a comparison: just as a mind overfull with business turns out dreams, a fool turns out a flood of words. Both are noise without substance, which is why 5:7 puts dreams, vapors and words together. The Targum keeps the comparison: a dream comes from a heart busy with much business. Its false prophets come in 5:7.

a: When you make a vow to God, do not be slow to pay it
t: Qohelet quotes the law of vows
p: This line closely follows Deuteronomy 23:21: when you vow, do not be slow to pay.
b: Deuteronomy 23:21 says: "When you make a vow to the LORD your God, do not be slow to pay it". Qohelet takes over the wording, and the Plain keeps the same English so the borrowing shows, but he changes "the LORD your God" to plain "God", as he does everywhere. A vow (neder) was a promise to give God something, usually an offering, if he answered a prayer: Jacob at Bethel (Genesis 28:20–22), Hannah for a son (1 Samuel 1:11), sailors saved from a storm (Jonah 1:16). Numbers 30:2 says that a man who vows "may not go back on his word". Jephthah's vow (Judges 11:30–39) shows how a rash vow could end in tragedy.
r: Deuteronomy 23:21–23; Numbers 30:2; Genesis 28:20–22; 1 Samuel 1:11; Judges 11:30–39; Psalm 66:13–14; Jonah 1:16

a: for fools give him no pleasure
p: The Hebrew says only 'there is no pleasure in fools'; whose pleasure is left unsaid.
b: Literally "for there is no pleasure in fools". The subject is not named, but the setting makes it God, as the Greek tradition and the Targum understand it ("the Lord has no pleasure in fools"). The word chefets, "pleasure, delight", turns up again in 5:8 in its late sense, "matter, business", and in 8:6. A fool here is the person who vows and then delays or forgets.

a: Not vowing is better than vowing and not paying.
t: Better not to vow at all?
p: The rabbis debated whether the ideal is not to vow at all, or to vow and pay.
b: Deuteronomy 23:22 already says that holding back from a vow is no sin. A teaching in the Talmud (Nedarim 9a) records a dispute over this verse. Rabbi Meir said that better than both (vowing and paying, or vowing and not paying) is not vowing at all; Rabbi Yehuda said that better than both is to vow and pay. Later Jewish practice grew wary of vows, and the Kol Nidre said before Yom Kippur asks release from vows rashly made. Jesus goes further on oaths: "do not take oaths at all" (Matthew 5:33–37; compare James 5:12). Christians have long disagreed over vows to God; see the "Where Christians differ" card on the chapter page.

a: bring sin on your own flesh
t: Your flesh: you, or your children?
p: 'Flesh' here means your own self; Rashi took it as your children.
b: "Flesh" (basar) often stands for the whole person, body and life (Psalm 63:1). The sense is: do not let a careless promise make you guilty. Rashi suggested that "your flesh" means your kin or children, as in Isaiah 58:7, so that a broken vow brings punishment on the family; the Targum makes it the judgment of Gehenna upon the flesh. The plain sense is the simpler one.
orig: לַחֲטִיא אֶת־בְּשָׂרֶךָ (lachati' 'et besarekha), 'to make your flesh sin'

a: the messenger
p: The Hebrew mal'akh can be a human messenger or an angel. The Greek and Syriac read 'God' instead.
b: Mal'akh means "messenger" and is also the word for an angel. Readers have taken it three ways. (1) A Temple official, perhaps a priest who came to collect what was vowed; Malachi 2:7 calls the priest "the messenger of the LORD of Armies", and Rashi thinks of the collector of pledged charity. (2) An angel who records or judges: Ibn Ezra, and the Targum, which makes him "the cruel angel" of the day of judgment. (3) God himself: the Greek and the Syriac read "before God", which may be an early explanation or a different Hebrew text (see the variant). The Plain keeps "the messenger", which leaves the options open.

a: "It was unintended."
t: The excuse of an unintended sin
p: Shegagah is the law's term for a sin done without meaning to, which a sacrifice could cover.
b: Shegagah is a technical word from the laws of sacrifice: a sin committed "unintentionally" (Leviticus 4:2, 22, 27; Numbers 15:22–29). For such sins the law provided a sin offering. Leviticus 5:4 even covers someone who swears an oath, "speaking rashly with his lips" (Leviticus 5:4), and only later realizes it. The fool in Qohelet uses the category as a loophole: he made a vow, fails to pay, and tells the Temple official it was a mistake, as if an offering would settle it. Qohelet's warning is that God hears the voice that made the promise.

a: there are vapors
p: Hevel, Qohelet's key word, is breath or vapor. This site renders it 'vapor' everywhere.
b: Hevel is the puff of breath you see on a cold morning, or a wisp of smoke: real, but brief and impossible to hold. Qohelet uses it some thirty-eight times. The Greek translated it mataiotes, "emptiness", and Jerome's Latin vanitas, which gave the KJV "vanity"; many modern versions say "meaningless" or "futile", and Michael Fox argues for "absurd", the gap between what should happen and what does. Each of these picks one side of the image (brevity, emptiness, frustration) and hides the others. The Plain keeps "vapor" in every verse, so the reader can see the same word return and judge its sense each time. Here the plural, "vapors", stands beside dreams and too many words: talk that evaporates. See the topic page on hevel.

a: But you, fear God.
p: Qohelet's answer to empty religion: the fear of God, which the epilogue makes the end of the matter.
b: The Hebrew puts God first for emphasis: "but God, fear!" Fearing God is one of Qohelet's steady themes (3:14; 7:18; 8:12–13), and the epilogue sums up the whole book as "fear God and keep his commands" (12:13). In Qohelet the fear of God is less a warm piety than a sober awe before a God who cannot be controlled, which leaves a person honest, humble and careful with words. The Targum turns the verse into a warning: do not believe the many dreams of false prophets and the vapors of sorcerers, but serve the wise and the righteous, and fear the LORD.

a: in the province
t: Officials above officials in the province
p: Medinah, 'province', is a term of the Persian empire, whose layers of officials taxed Judea.
b: Medinah is the word for a district of an empire: Judah was such a province in the Persian period (Ezra 2:1; Nehemiah 1:3; Nehemiah 7:6), and Esther counts 127 of them (Esther 1:1). Qohelet describes a world of layered officials: local tax collectors, governors, satraps and the distant king, each watching the one below. In such a system the poor at the bottom are squeezed and justice gets lost. The same picture fits the Ptolemaic Greek rule of the 200s BC, whose papyri show a dense bureaucracy of agents and inspectors, and some scholars prefer that date. Either way, Qohelet's first readers knew this world.
r: 2:8; 4:1; Ezra 2:1; Nehemiah 1:3; Nehemiah 5:4; Nehemiah 5:15; Esther 1:1; Esther 1:22

a: another one is watching
p: The 'watching' may be officials protecting each other, spying on each other, or God above them all.
b: The verb shamar means to watch, guard or keep. (1) Cynically: each official covers for the one below him, so the system protects itself, and you should not be surprised by injustice. (2) Each official watches the one below for his own profit, so the poor are squeezed at every level. (3) The pious reading of the Targum and Rashi: the highest "high one" is God, who sees, and the "higher ones" are his agents who will punish in time. The plural gevohim, "high ones", could even be a plural of majesty for God. Most modern commentators take (1) or (2), since "do not be shocked" suggests resignation, not comfort.
orig: גָבֹהַּ מֵעַל גָּבֹהַּ שֹׁמֵר (gavoah me'al gavoah shomer)

a: a king for the farmed field
t: One of the hardest verses in the book
p: The Hebrew can mean a king devoted to farming, a king served by the field, or a king who is himself a servant.
b: Word for word: "and the gain of a land in all, it; a king to a field is served." (The written text has the feminine "it" and the reading tradition the masculine; the sense is the same.) (1) Some read it as praise of order: a land does well with a king who cares for its farmland. (2) The KJV reads "the king himself is served by the field": even a king lives off the farmer. (3) Others read it as part of the complaint of 5:8: the king is the last of the officials who live off the field. The Greek has "a king of the worked field", and the Targum makes it a story of a king who flees and has to serve a farmer. No reading is certain. The Plain stays close to the words.

a: The lover of silver never gets his fill of silver
p: Silver here is money. Qohelet's point, that loving it never satisfies, runs through the New Testament.
b: Kesef is silver, and so money, since silver was weighed out as currency before and alongside coins (Persian and then Greek coins were in use in Judea in Qohelet's time). Qohelet says that loving money is self-defeating: the appetite for it grows faster than the supply. Jesus warns that life does not consist in the abundance of possessions (Luke 12:15), and 1 Timothy 6:10 calls the love of money a root of all kinds of evil, using a Greek word, philargyria, "love of silver", that matches Qohelet's phrase. The Targum adds that a rich man's money earns no reward in the world to come unless he gives it to charity.

a: the more mouths eat them up
p: A rich household drew servants, guests, relatives and tax collectors, all eating from the same store.
b: In the ancient world wealth meant a large household: servants and slaves, hangers-on, guests to impress, and officials who expected their share. As income rose, so did the number of people living off it. Qohelet's owner ends up with nothing but the view. The word for what the owner gets, kishron, means "success" or "advantage" and appears only in Qohelet (2:21; 4:4; 5:11). The written text has "the appearance of" and the reading tradition "the seeing of" his eyes; both mean the same.

a: the rich man's fullness
t: A full belly, or a full purse?
p: Hassava', 'fullness', can be a stomach too full to sleep or wealth too worrying to sleep.
b: Hassava' means being full or sated. It may be the rich man's heavy dinner, which keeps him awake, in contrast to the worker who sleeps whether he ate little or much. Or it may be his abundance of wealth, which leaves him anxious. Hebrew can carry both at once, and the Plain's "fullness" keeps both. The Greek read the worker ('oved) as "the slave" ('eved), a difference of one vowel in the same letters (see the variant).

a: a sickening evil
p: Ra'ah cholah, 'a sick evil', is Qohelet's phrase for a wrong that makes you ill to see. It returns in 5:16.
b: Cholah is the word for sickness: the evil is "sick" or "sickening" (compare 6:2, "a sickness, an evil one"). The KJV's "sore evil" uses an older sense of "sore", painful. Qohelet's case is a man who saves his riches, only to lose them in one bad deal, so that his son inherits nothing (5:14).

a: lost in an evil task
t: An evil task, or a bad deal
p: The same words as the 'evil task' of 1:13 and 4:8; here they describe a business venture gone wrong.
b: 'Inyan ra' is the phrase Qohelet uses for the "evil task" God gave humanity (1:13) and for the lonely man's endless toil (4:8). Here it names the occasion of the loss: a bad venture, an unlucky deal, a trade that failed. The Plain keeps the same English so the reader can hear the echo: the whole human business is an evil task, and this is one small piece of it. The Greek has "in an evil distraction" (perispasmos), its regular word for 'inyan.

a: Just as he came out of his mother's womb, naked
t: Naked he came, naked he goes
p: Qohelet echoes Job: 'Naked I came out from my mother's womb, and naked I will return there.'
b: Job said, "Naked I came out from my mother's womb, / and naked I will return there" (Job 1:21), and then blessed the LORD. Qohelet uses the same picture with no blessing: the man who lost his fortune leaves the world as empty-handed as he entered it, and so does everyone. Psalm 49:17 says the rich man takes nothing with him when he dies, and 1 Timothy 6:7 says we brought nothing into the world and can carry nothing out. "Return" to the mother's womb is a picture of the earth as the mother of all (compare Sirach 40:1).

a: Of all his toil he will carry off nothing to take away in his hand
t: You cannot take it with you: an Egyptian harper's song
p: An Egyptian tomb song makes the same point. The likeness is real; borrowing cannot be shown.
b: Egyptian harpers' songs, sung at banquets and carved in tombs, urge listeners to enjoy life because death takes everything. The Song from the Tomb of King Intef, known from a New Kingdom papyrus, says that no one is allowed to take his goods with him, and that no one who departs comes back again (in Lichtheim's translation). Like Qohelet, it moves from that fact to a call to enjoy the day (compare 5:18). What the parallel shows: Qohelet shares a theme that thinkers across the ancient Near East put into words. What it does not show: that he knew this song. The Egyptian song points to the tomb and its rites; Qohelet points to God, who gives the days and the share (5:18–19).

a: he toils for the wind
p: Working for wind means working for something you can never hold, like 'chasing the wind'.
b: Wind (ruach) is Qohelet's other picture for what slips away, close to vapor (hevel): all is "vapor and chasing the wind" (1:14; 2:11). Here the image is bitter: a man has spent his life working for wind. The question "What gain is there?" takes up the book's opening question (1:3; 3:9). Proverbs 11:29 says that the one who troubles his household will inherit wind.

a: he eats in darkness all his days
p: The miser eats in the dark, alone and joyless. The Greek and a Dead Sea Scroll read the line differently.
b: To eat "in darkness" may picture a man too stingy to light a lamp, or a life of gloom, or eating alone and in secret, as the Targum puts it ("that he may eat his bread alone"). It is the opposite of the picture that follows in 5:18: eating and drinking and seeing good. The Greek reads "all his days are in darkness and in mourning", and the Dead Sea Scroll 4QQoh-a has no word "eats" at all; many scholars think the original was "in darkness and mourning" (see the variant). The Plain follows the Leningrad Codex.

a: eat and drink and see good in all his toil
t: The call to enjoy: preacher of joy, or of resignation?
p: The fourth of seven passages that tell readers to enjoy what God gives. Scholars weigh them differently.
b: Qohelet returns again and again to eating, drinking and seeing good in one's toil (2:24–26; 3:12–13; 3:22; 5:18–20; 8:15; 9:7–10; 11:7–10). R. N. Whybray called him a "preacher of joy": these passages grow stronger through the book and are its positive message. Michael Fox reads them as the best that can be salvaged in an absurd world, a small consolation, not a solution. Others, such as Tremper Longman, hear a man who settles for pleasure because he has found nothing better. The wording here is close to 3:13, with "good and beautiful" added; "beautiful" (yafeh) is the word of 3:11, "Everything he has made beautiful in its time."

a: For that is his share.
p: Cheleq is a portion or allotment, something given. Qohelet sets it against yitron, a gain that lasts.
b: Cheleq is the share of plunder or the plot of land that falls to someone (Genesis 14:24; Joshua 18:7). Qohelet uses it for what a person receives in life: food, drink, work and joy (2:10; 3:22; 9:9). It differs from "gain" (yitron), the lasting profit he says no one has (1:3; 5:16). The share is limited and temporary, but it is real and it is God's gift. In 9:6 the dead have no more share in anything done under the sun.

a: God keeps him busy with the joy of his heart
p: Ma'aneh can mean that God occupies a person with joy, or that God answers him through joy.
b: The Hebrew ma'aneh can come from a verb "to be busy" (as in 'inyan, "task") or from "to answer". (1) "Keeps him busy": joy so fills a person's days that he does not dwell on how short they are, the reading of Fox and many others; the Greek has "God distracts him". (2) "Answers him": Norbert Lohfink argued that God reveals himself to a person through the joy of the heart, so joy is a kind of answer from God. The Plain follows the first, which fits the Greek and the context of busyness (5:3), and gives the second here.

a: a foreigner eats it instead
p: Nokhri is a foreigner, someone outside the family. The man's wealth goes to a stranger.
b: Nokhri means a foreigner, someone of another people (Ruth 2:10), not merely another person. The rich man of 6:2 lacks nothing, yet someone outside his family eats what he gathered. Qohelet does not say how: no heir, a creditor, a conqueror, a royal confiscation. The Targum spins a story: he dies childless, his kinsman refuses to take the inheritance, and his widow marries a stranger who consumes it. In a province under foreign rule (5:8), the picture of outsiders eating the land's produce was not abstract.

a: Yet God does not let him be master of it
t: The curse of the eaten harvest
p: Deuteronomy warns that foreigners will eat what Israel worked for. Qohelet finds this happening to anyone.
b: The covenant curses of Deuteronomy include this one: "A people you have never known will eat what your soil grows and everything you have worked for" (Deuteronomy 28:33; compare Deuteronomy 28:30–31; Amos 5:11). There it is punishment for disobedience. Qohelet sees it happen without explanation, and he says plainly that God is the one who gives the wealth and God is the one who does not grant the power to enjoy it. The same verb, "let him be master" (hishlit), describes the happy case in 5:19. The contrast between the two verses is the point.

a: His appetite
p: Nefesh is often 'soul' in older English. In 6:2–9 it is the appetite, the craving self.
b: Nefesh is the throat, the breath, the life, and so the self with its desires. Older versions often render it "soul" (KJV "his soul"), which suggests a part of a person that lives on after death; Qohelet means the hungry self that wants and is never filled. The word runs through this chapter: the appetite lacks nothing (6:2), does not get its fill of good (6:3), is never filled up (6:7), and goes roaming after more (6:9). The Plain renders it "appetite" each time so the thread can be seen.

a: he does not even have a burial
p: To lie unburied was a disgrace and a curse. Why a man with a hundred children would lack a burial is unclear.
b: A proper burial, with mourning and a family tomb, was the honorable end of a life (Genesis 25:8–9). To be left unburied was the fate of the cursed: Jezebel (2 Kings 9:35–37), King Jehoiakim, given "the burial of a donkey" (Jeremiah 22:19), the fallen king of Babylon (Isaiah 14:19–20). It is strange for a father of a hundred children, which is part of the point: even the greatest blessings do not guarantee a good end. Some scholars think the clause belongs with the stillborn child of the next lines, which was often buried without rites; the Targum makes it a man who never prepared himself a grave.

a: the baby born dead
p: Nefel, 'one that falls', is a miscarried or stillborn child. Job used the same picture in his despair.
b: Nefel comes from the verb "to fall": a child that falls from the womb before its time. Job wished he had been "like a stillbirth tucked away, / like babies who have never seen the light" (Job 3:16), and Psalm 58:8 uses the image in a curse. Qohelet's judgment is cold: a long life without satisfaction is worse than no life at all, because the stillborn at least has rest (6:5). He made a similar judgment in 4:2–3, where the one who never existed is better off than the living.

a: and darkness covers its name
p: The stillborn has no name and no memory. 'Name' in Hebrew means a person's lasting presence.
b: In Hebrew thought a name is how a person lives on: in the family line, in memory, in reputation (7:1). The stillborn child is not even named. It comes "in vapor", a breath, and goes into darkness. The words "vapor" and "darkness" are Qohelet's words for the whole of life (5:17; 11:8), so the child's brief existence is a small version of everyone's.

a: does not everything go to one place?
p: The same words as 3:20: everything goes to one place, the grave.
b: The one place is the grave, or Sheol, the world of the dead (see 3:20 and 9:10). The question makes the long life of the rich man and the brief one of the stillborn equal in the end: both arrive at the same destination. A thousand years twice over is longer than Methuselah's 969 (Genesis 5:27). The Targum, which reads the book with judgment after death in mind, makes the one place Gehenna, where sinners go. The chapter page and the notes at 3:16–22 and 9:1–10 discuss how this verse is used in arguments about life after death.

a: All the toil of a human being goes to feed his mouth
p: A saying close to Proverbs 16:26: the mouth drives the worker, and the appetite is never filled.
b: Proverbs says: "A laborer's appetite labors on his behalf, / because his mouth presses him hard" (Proverbs 16:26). There the hungry mouth is a good motive. Qohelet takes the same observation and draws a gloomier conclusion: work feeds the mouth, but the appetite (nefesh) is never filled up, like Sheol and death in Proverbs 27:20 and Habakkuk 2:5. The verse may be a common proverb that Qohelet quotes.

a: though he knows how to walk his way in front of the living
p: The Hebrew is unclear. It may mean that even a poor man with good manners gains nothing lasting.
b: Word for word: "what to the poor man knowing to walk before the living?" (1) The poor man who knows how to conduct himself in society, perhaps wisely and properly, still has no edge (taking the question from the first half of the verse). (2) What advantage does a poor man have over the rich, if he knows how to get on in life? (3) The Greek reads "because the poor man knows how to walk before life". The Targum makes him study the Law to learn how to walk before the righteous in paradise. Most scholars take the verse as a double question with the answer "none".
orig: מַה־לֶּעָנִי יוֹדֵעַ לַהֲלֹךְ נֶגֶד הַחַיִּים (mah le'ani yodea' lahalokh neged hachayyim)

a: What the eyes see is better than an appetite on the move
p: Better to enjoy what is in front of you than to let your desire wander after what you do not have.
b: "The sight of the eyes" is what you can actually see and have; "the going of the appetite" is desire roaming after more. The English proverb "a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush" catches the sense. Then Qohelet adds that even this good advice is vapor and chasing the wind, the refrain that has closed many sections since 1:14. Addison Wright argued that this refrain marks the end of the first half of the book; see the chapter page.
orig: טוֹב מַרְאֵה עֵינַיִם מֵהֲלָךְ־נָפֶשׁ (tov mar'eh 'enayim mehalokh-nafesh)

a: It is known what a human being is
t: Named long ago, and only human
p: To name is to define. What humans are was settled long ago: Adam, from the ground, weaker than God.
b: In the Bible to name something is to fix what it is (Genesis 1:5; Genesis 2:19–20; Isaiah 40:26). Whatever exists has had its nature settled. The word for a human being, 'adam, recalls Adam made from the ground ('adamah, Genesis 2:7), and many readers hear the echo: we are earth. The "one who is stronger" is most likely God, whom no human can take to court (Job 9:32–33; Isaiah 45:9); the Targum says so outright. The written text has "who makes himself strong", the reading tradition "who is stronger"; the sense is the same.

a: which he spends like a shadow
p: A shadow has shape but no substance, and it moves on. The psalms and Job use the same picture.
b: Psalm 144:4 says: "A human is like a puff of air; / his days are a shadow that slips past", setting hevel and shadow side by side as Qohelet does. Job says a human being "like a shadow ... runs off, and he does not stay" (Job 14:2), and David prays that our days on earth are like a shadow (1 Chronicles 29:15). James 4:14 compares life to a mist that appears and then vanishes. Qohelet adds the two questions that drive the second half of the book: who knows what is good, and who can tell what comes after?

a: Who can tell a person what will come after him under the sun?
p: Does 'after him' mean after his death, or after his time on earth among the living?
b: Qohelet asks this question three times (3:22; 6:12; 10:14; compare 7:14; 8:7), and the Plain keeps "who can tell him" and "what will come after him" wherever the Hebrew repeats. Most commentators take it to mean what will happen on earth after a person dies: who will inherit, whether his work will last (2:18–19). The words "under the sun" support this. Jewish and Christian readers have also heard a question about life beyond death, which the Targum answers by pointing to the study of the Law and the world to come. Qohelet himself leaves it as a question.

a: Better a good name than good oil
t: Name and oil: a play on words
p: Shem, 'name', and shemen, 'oil', sound alike. Fragrant oil was a luxury; a good name lasts longer.
b: The Hebrew is a neat sound-play: tov shem mishemen tov, "good is a name, more than good oil". Fine olive oil, often perfumed, was used to anoint guests, kings and the dead, and its scent filled a house; the Song of Songs compares a lover's name to oil poured out (Song of Songs 1:3). A good reputation is better because it lasts and spreads further. Ecclesiastes Rabbah lists the contrasts: oil runs down, a good name rises; oil costs money, a good name is free; oil is for the living, a good name for the living and the dead.
orig: טוֹב שֵׁם מִשֶּׁמֶן טוֹב (tov shem mishemen tov)

a: and the day of death than the day he was born
t: Better the day of death: Greek parallels
p: Greek writers also said death, or never being born, is better. The likeness is in the thought, not the words.
b: Herodotus tells of the brothers Cleobis and Biton, whose reward from the gods was to die in their sleep at the height of their honor, a sign that death is better for a man than life (Histories 1.31); he also describes a Thracian tribe that mourned at births and rejoiced at burials (5.4). The poet Theognis and the chorus of Sophocles' Oedipus at Colonus say that best of all is not to be born. What this shows: Qohelet's saying belongs to a mood shared around the eastern Mediterranean. What it does not show: direct borrowing. Qohelet's reason is different: the day of death completes a life and its name (7:1a), and it teaches the living (7:2). He still says elsewhere that "light is sweet" (11:7).

a: a house where people mourn
t: The house of mourning and the drinking house
p: Mourning lasted days, with neighbors coming to comfort; a mishteh was a feast with wine.
b: When someone died, family and neighbors gathered at the house to weep, to sit with the mourners and to bring food, often for seven days (Genesis 50:10; 1 Samuel 31:13; Sirach 22:12). The "house where they drink" is a bet mishteh, a feast where wine flowed. Qohelet's advice is not to avoid feasts (he urges eating and drinking in 9:7) but to go where death is faced honestly, since that is "the end of every human being". The Targum sees the righteous man in the house of mourning take death to heart and repent.

a: Grief is better than laughter
t: Grief or joy? A contradiction the rabbis noticed
p: Ka'as is 'frustration' in 1:18 and 2:23. Here it is the sorrow of 7:2. The rabbis set it against 2:2 and 8:15.
b: Ka'as covers vexation, grief and anger: "frustration" in 1:18 and 2:23, "anger" in 7:9, and here the sadness of the house of mourning. The Talmud (Shabbat 30b) lists this verse among the contradictions that made some sages want to withdraw the book: "grief is better than laughter" against 2:2, which the Talmud reads as "of laughter I said, it is praiseworthy" (taking mehulal as "praised", not "madness"), and "I spoke in praise of joy" (8:15) against "about joy, 'What does this accomplish?'" (2:2). The sages resolved them by reading one side of each pair as God's anger (ka'as) toward the righteous in this world or the joy of keeping a command. The book introduction discusses the debate. The Targum reads 7:3 the same way.

a: For like the crackle of thorns beneath the pot
p: Another sound-play: sirim, 'thorns', under the sir, 'pot'. Thorns burn fast and loud, and give little heat.
b: The Hebrew plays on two words that sound almost the same: hassirim, "the thorns", and hassir, "the pot". Dry thorn bushes were cheap kindling. They catch at once, crackle and pop, and burn out before the pot boils (compare Psalm 58:9; Psalm 118:12). The fool's laughter is like that: loud, quick and useless. English cannot keep the pun; one paraphrase that tries is "like nettles under a kettle".
orig: כְקוֹל הַסִּירִים תַּחַת הַסִּיר (keqol hassirim tachat hassir)

a: For oppression makes a fool of the wise
p: The wise man may be the victim or the one who profits. A scroll from Qumran may read 'twists' for 'ruins'.
b: 'Osheq is oppression or extortion (the same root as "oppression" in 4:1 and 5:8). Two readings: the wise man is driven to madness by being oppressed, or he is corrupted by gaining from oppression, which suits the parallel line about a "gift" (mattanah), a bribe that ruins the heart (Exodus 23:8; Deuteronomy 16:19). The verse begins with "for", which does not fit well after 7:6, and some scholars think a line has dropped out before it. In the Dead Sea Scroll 4QQoh-a the verb of the second line is only partly preserved; the editors restore it as wy'wh, "and twists", in place of "and ruins". The Greek has "destroys the heart of his vigor".
orig: כִּי הָעֹשֶׁק יְהוֹלֵל חָכָם (ki ha'osheq yeholel chakham)

a: a long-suffering spirit is better than a lofty one
p: Literally 'long of spirit' and 'high of spirit'. Proverbs praises the slow-to-anger in the same terms.
b: "Long of spirit" ('erekh ruach) is patience, the human version of God's being "slow to anger" ('erekh 'appayim, Exodus 34:6). "High of spirit" (gevah ruach) is pride (Proverbs 16:18). Proverbs says "Being slow to anger is better than being a mighty soldier" (Proverbs 16:32; compare Proverbs 14:29). The first half of the verse, that the end is better than the beginning, ties patience to time: wait and see how a matter ends.

a: How is it that the earlier days were better than these days?
p: Qohelet forbids nostalgia. He has already said no one remembers the past rightly (1:11).
b: The question sounds pious, but Qohelet calls it unwise. Part of the reason is in 1:9–11: nothing is new, and no one truly remembers the past, so the "good old days" are partly a fiction. Part is practical: complaining about the present does not help a person live in it. Readers in a province under foreign rule, remembering the kingdom of David and Solomon (compare Haggai 2:3; Ezra 3:12), may have been tempted to such talk. The Targum, by contrast, says the former generations really were better because their deeds were better.

a: Wisdom along with an inheritance is good
t: Wisdom with, or like, an inheritance
p: 'Im can mean 'with' or 'as good as'. Either way Qohelet ties wisdom to money in the next verse.
b: The preposition 'im usually means "with": wisdom is good, especially when you also have an inheritance, a worldly-wise view. It can also mean "like, as" (Job 9:26; Psalm 106:6), giving "wisdom is as good as an inheritance". The KJV has "Wisdom is good with an inheritance". "Those who see the sun" are the living (11:7; compare 6:5). Verse 12 explains with an image of shade.

a: For to be in wisdom's shade
t: The shade of wisdom and money
p: In a hot land shade means protection. Wisdom shelters you like money does, but wisdom also gives life.
b: Shade (tsel) is a common image for protection (Numbers 14:9; Psalm 121:5; Isaiah 30:2). Qohelet says that being under wisdom's protection is like being under money's: both shelter a person. Then he names wisdom's edge: it "gives life", the promise of Proverbs that wisdom is a tree of life (Proverbs 3:18; Proverbs 8:35). The Hebrew repeats "in the shade"; the Greek and the Syriac read "like the shade" in one place (see the variant).
orig: בְּצֵל הַחָכְמָה בְּצֵל הַכָּסֶף (betsel hachokhmah betsel hakkasef)

a: Who is able to set straight what he has bent?
p: A return to 1:15, now with God named as the one who bent it.
b: In 1:15 Qohelet quoted a saying: "The bent cannot be set straight." Here he says who bent it: God. What God has done, no one can undo (3:14; Job 12:14; Isaiah 14:27). The verse is not a charge that God is crooked, but an admission that some things in life are bent beyond human repair, and that a wise person accepts the limit. The Targum applies it to people born blind or lame, whom only God could straighten.

a: God made this one to match that one
p: Good days and bad days both come from God. Isaiah and Job say the same, and Sirach builds on it.
b: Qohelet's God makes both: "I make peace and create disaster" (Isaiah 45:7); "Should we take the good from God, and not take the bad too?" (Job 2:10; compare Lamentations 3:38). Sirach later develops the idea that God's works come in pairs, each the opposite of the other (Sirach 33:14–15). The purpose clause is debated: God mixes the days so that humans cannot predict the future, or so that they cannot find fault with him, or (in the Targum) so that no evil will be found in the world to come. The practical advice is simple: enjoy the good day, and think hard on the bad one.

a: There is a righteous man who dies in his righteousness
t: The righteous dying, the wicked living long
p: The preposition 'in' can mean 'in spite of' or even 'because of'. Qohelet challenges the promise of Proverbs.
b: Proverbs teaches that the fear of the LORD lengthens life and the years of the wicked are cut short (Proverbs 10:27). Qohelet has seen the opposite. The verb 'oved means "perishes, dies": the righteous man's life is cut off, while the wicked man's lasts. The Hebrew "in his righteousness" may mean "in spite of" it, or bitterly, "because of" it. The complaint is old: Jeremiah 12:1 asks why the way of the wicked prospers, Job 21:7 why the wicked live on, and Psalm 73 almost lost its faith over the same sight. "My days of vapor" may mean "my brief life" or "my life of frustration". Qohelet returns to the problem in 8:14.

a: Do not be righteous too much
p: This verse has been read as a call to moderation, a warning against self-righteousness, or a cynical shrug.
b: Moderation. Many readers hear the Greek "nothing in excess": keep to a middle way between strictness and sin (compare Aristotle's mean). False righteousness. R. N. Whybray argued that the verbs mean claiming righteousness and posing as wise: Qohelet warns against those who think their piety guarantees reward (7:15). Rabbinic readings. The Talmud (Yoma 22b) hears it as a word to Saul, who spared Agag out of misplaced mercy (1 Samuel 15), and Rashi follows; the Targum warns judges against pitying a man justly condemned. Worldly prudence. Others hear something close to a shrug: do not be a saint or a great sinner, because either can get you killed. 7:20 shows that Qohelet does not think anyone is too righteous in fact.

a: Why bring ruin on yourself?
p: Tishshomem can mean 'be destroyed' or 'be appalled'. Either fits the warning.
b: The verb shamem means to be desolate or ruined, and also to be stunned or appalled (Isaiah 52:14; Ezra 9:3). Qohelet may mean that excessive strictness destroys a person, or that it leaves him confounded when life does not reward it (7:15). The reflexive form here, found only in this verse in Qohelet, suggests ruin brought on oneself.

a: Why die when it is not your time?
p: Everything has its time, including death (3:2). The wicked and the fool can hasten theirs.
b: Qohelet has said there is "a time to die" (3:2). He does not claim that the wicked always die young (7:15 says the opposite), but that wickedness and folly put a person in danger of an early death, as Proverbs teaches: "the wicked find their years shortened" (Proverbs 10:27; compare Psalm 55:23). Notice that he does not say "be a little wicked": the second line, "do not be a fool", matches "do not act the wise man to excess" in 7:16.

a: For the one who fears God will come through all of them
p: Yetse' 'et kullam may mean escape both extremes, or fulfill both duties.
b: Literally "will go out with all of them". (1) The God-fearer escapes the dangers of both extremes in 7:16–17. (2) In later Hebrew yatsa' means to fulfill a duty, so he does justice to both sides, as the Targum takes it ("performs the duty of both"). (3) He goes forward holding both, without being trapped by either. In each reading the fear of God, not a calculated balance, is what keeps a person safe.

a: than ten rulers who are in a city
p: Ten may be a round number for a full council of leading men, as in Ruth 4:2.
b: Ten was a common number for a body of elders or a quorum (Genesis 18:32; Ruth 4:2). A city ruled by a council of leading men, rather than a king, fits the cities of the Persian and Greek periods. The point is that one person's wisdom gives more strength than the whole city government. Proverbs 21:22 and Ecclesiastes 9:13–16 tell the same truth as a story: a wise man takes a strong city, or a poor wise man saves one. The Targum turns the verse into the story of Joseph and his ten brothers.

a: For there is no human being on the earth so righteous that he does good and does not sin
t: No one who does not sin
p: Qohelet agrees with Solomon's prayer and the psalms. Paul's 'no one righteous' may echo this verse.
b: Solomon's prayer at the Temple says "there is no human being who never sins" (1 Kings 8:46), and Psalm 143:2 says that "no living person is in the right" before God (compare Proverbs 20:9). Paul's list of verses in Romans 3:10–18 opens, "There is no righteous person, not one" (Romans 3:10). That line is usually traced to Psalm 14:1–3, but its word "righteous" (dikaios) is in the Greek of this verse and not in the psalm, so some scholars think Paul has Ecclesiastes 7:20 in mind as well. In context Qohelet's point is practical: since no one is sinless, do not be "righteous too much" (7:16), and do not take every curse to heart (7:21–22). See the "Where Christians differ" card on the chapter page.
r: 1 Kings 8:46; Psalm 143:2; Proverbs 20:9; Psalm 14:1–3; Romans 3:10–12; Romans 3:23; 1 John 1:8

a: or you may hear your slave cursing you
p: If you listen for every word said about you, you will hear things you would rather not.
b: 'Eved means a slave or servant (see 2:7). A household slave knew his master's faults and might curse him in private. Qohelet's advice is not to go looking for what people say. Proverbs warns "Do not run down a servant to his master, / or he will curse you" (Proverbs 30:10). Verse 22 turns the point around: you have done the same to others.

a: "Let me become wise."
p: The king of 1:12–2:26 speaks again: even he could not get wisdom in hand.
b: Qohelet speaks in the voice of the king who "gained wisdom beyond all" (1:16; compare 1 Kings 4:29–34). Now he confesses that wisdom stayed far away. Jewish tradition read this as Solomon admitting that he could not understand some commands of the Law, such as the red heifer of Numbers 19 (Ecclesiastes Rabbah on this verse; compare Talmud, Yoma 14a). Job 28 asks the same question: "But wisdom: where can it be found?" (Job 28:12).

a: and deep, deep down
p: Hebrew doubles a word to make it extreme: 'deep, deep' means unfathomably deep.
b: Doubling, as in 'amoq 'amoq, is Hebrew's way of saying "very" (compare "bad, bad" in Proverbs 20:14). "Whatever has been" renders mah-shehayah, the same Hebrew as in 1:9, 3:15 and 6:10: the whole of what exists and happens. Paul sounds a similar note of wonder at the depth of God's wealth, wisdom and knowledge (Romans 11:33), though Paul finds it worth praising and Qohelet finds it out of reach.

a: a reckoning
t: A reckoning: the language of accounts
p: Cheshbon is an accountant's word: a reckoning or total. It returns in 7:27 and 9:10, and as 'schemes' in 7:29.
b: Cheshbon means a reckoning, a sum, an account. Qohelet speaks like a bookkeeper: he wants to add things up and get the total of life (7:27, "adding one to one to find the reckoning"). The Plain renders it "reckoning" in all three places where it occurs: here, in 7:27, and in 9:10 ("no doing and no reckoning" in Sheol). Then, in 7:29, the plural chishshevonot turns up for human "schemes", the clever devices people invent, as in 2 Chronicles 26:15, where it names war machines. The search for the reckoning ends by finding that humans make reckonings of their own.

a: the woman who is a hunter's trap
t: The woman more bitter than death
p: Is this a judgment on women, on one kind of woman, on Folly, or a view Qohelet quotes and then rejects?
b: Read on its own, the verse condemns "the woman" as a deadly trap. Readers have taken it four ways. (1) A judgment on women, and many feminist and other critics say plainly that 7:26–28 is misogynist. (2) One kind of woman: the seductress of Proverbs, whose end is "bitter as wormwood" (Proverbs 5:4) and whose house is a trap (Proverbs 7:23; Proverbs 22:14); so many commentators, noting that Qohelet urges his reader to see "life with a woman you love" (9:9), where the Hebrew has no article, against "the woman" here. (3) A figure: Woman Folly (Proverbs 9:13), or for Rashi, heresy; the Targum makes her a bad wife whom the righteous divorce. (4) A quotation: Norbert Lohfink and others read 7:26 as a common saying that Qohelet tests and dismantles in 7:27–29, ending in a verdict about all humankind. The notes at 7:28–29 continue.

a: more bitter than death
p: The Talmud names death the hardest of ten hard things (Bava Batra 10a); Rashi cites it here.
b: Mar, "bitter", is the taste of wormwood and of grief (Ruth 1:20; 1 Samuel 15:32). The Talmud (Bava Batra 10a) lists ten hard things in the world, each overcome by the next, with death the hardest; Rashi cites it here. The images that follow come from hunting and fishing: metsodim, snares or hunting nets; charamim, nets (the word is used of fishing nets in Habakkuk 1:15); and 'asurim, bonds that tie a prisoner.

a: See, this is what I have found
p: Only here in the body of the book does another voice say 'says Qohelet', and the verb is feminine.
b: The book's outer voice, the frame narrator, speaks of Qohelet in the third person at the start and end (1:1–2; 12:8–14). Only here, in the middle of a first-person passage, does that voice break in: "says Qohelet". Michael Fox argues that this shows the whole book is presented as a report about Qohelet by another writer. The verb is feminine, 'amrah. "Qohelet" has a feminine form, like titles of office such as hassoferet, "the scribe" (Ezra 2:55), so the verb may agree with the form. But elsewhere the verb is masculine (1:2; 12:8), and the Greek and Syriac read it so here. Many scholars think the letters were once divided as "says the Qohelet" (see the variant). Rashi took the feminine as "wisdom" speaking.

a: One man out of a thousand I have found
p: 'Adam can mean a human being or a man. The saying may be the proverb Qohelet quotes in order to answer it.
b: 'Adam is usually "a human being", but here it stands against "a woman", so it seems to mean a man. "One in a thousand" is a proverbial rarity (Job 33:23; Deuteronomy 32:30). Readers have long noticed that Solomon, in whose voice Qohelet speaks, had seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, a thousand women (1 Kings 11:3). Rashi turns the verse into a saying about students: of a thousand who begin Scripture, one becomes a judge. Ecclesiastes Rabbah takes the man as Abraham and the woman as Sarah. Those who read 7:26–28 as a quoted view note how Qohelet phrases it: "something I am still seeking ... and have not found", which sounds like failure, not proof. The next verse is his conclusion.

a: God made human beings straight
p: 'Adam here is all humankind, men and women, as in Genesis 1:27. The fault lies with all of 'them'.
b: The word is again 'adam, but now with the plural "they": humankind as a whole, as in "So God created the human in his image ... male and female he created them" (Genesis 1:27). God made them yashar, straight or upright; they went after schemes. Whatever 7:26–28 said about men and women, Qohelet's final finding puts all human beings in the same place. Ecclesiastes Rabbah connects it with the fall: Adam was upright, and "when they became two", they sought many schemes (Genesis 3). Christian readers have used the verse for the teaching that God created humans good and sin came after (compare Augustine, City of God 14.11).

a: Who knows how to interpret a matter?
p: Pesher, 'interpretation', is an Aramaic word, found only here in Hebrew. Daniel and the Qumran scrolls use it.
b: The noun pesher appears nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible. Its Aramaic form pishra is Daniel's word for interpreting dreams and the writing on the wall (Daniel 2:4–7; Daniel 4:18; Daniel 5:15–16), and the Hebrew form names the Dead Sea Scrolls commentaries that interpret the prophets, such as the Pesher on Habakkuk. It is one of the late words that help scholars date Qohelet's Hebrew (see the book introduction). Who can interpret a "matter" (davar, a word or a thing) is the courtier's skill, the ability to read a king's words and a situation, which leads into the advice on kings that follows.

a: Wisdom lights up a person's face
t: A face that shines, a hard face softened
p: Wisdom brightens a face, as God's favor does. 'Strength of face' is boldness or insolence.
b: A shining face is a sign of favor and life: "May the LORD make his face shine toward you" (Numbers 6:25), and Moses' face shone after speaking with God (Exodus 34:29). "Strength of face" ('oz panim) is a brazen, hard look: the fierce nation of Deuteronomy 28:50, the seductress who "puts on a hard face" (Proverbs 7:13), and the wicked man of Proverbs 21:29. The Plain renders it "the stern look on his face". Wisdom changes it, perhaps teaching the courtier to hide a stern look before the king. The Greek and Syriac read the last word differently, "and the bold of face will be hated" (see the variant).
r: Numbers 6:25; Exodus 34:29–30; Deuteronomy 28:50; Proverbs 7:13; Proverbs 21:29; Daniel 8:23

a: do what the king's mouth tells you
p: Literally 'keep the king's mouth'. Qohelet speaks to men who served at a royal court.
b: "Keep the mouth of the king" means obey his spoken order (compare Genesis 45:21, where Joseph acts "At Pharaoh's word", literally "by the mouth of Pharaoh"). The advice of 8:2–6 fits courtiers and officials who had to deal with an absolute ruler: Persian kings, or Ptolemaic and Seleucid kings, who could not be questioned (8:4; compare Esther 4:11; Daniel 3). The verse begins oddly with "I", which the Plain renders "I say"; the Greek and Syriac lack it (see the variant). Rashi applies the verse in two ways: to the commands of God, the true King, and to the rulers of the nations, whom Israel obeys in taxes but not in idolatry, as the three young men told Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 3:16–18).
r: Genesis 45:21; Esther 4:11; Daniel 3:16–18; Proverbs 24:21; Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:13–17

a: with God's oath in mind
p: An oath of loyalty to the king sworn before God, God's own oath to the king, or Israel's oath at Sinai.
b: "The oath of God" (shevu'at Elohim) can be (1) an oath of loyalty sworn to the king in God's name, as officials pledged themselves to Solomon (1 Chronicles 29:24) and Zedekiah swore to Nebuchadnezzar by God (Ezekiel 17:13–19; 2 Chronicles 36:13); (2) God's oath to the king's house (2 Samuel 7; Psalm 89:3, 35), so that obedience honors God's choice; or (3), for Rashi, the oath Israel swore at Sinai to keep God's commands, which limits what the king can demand. Most modern scholars take the first.
orig: וְעַל דִּבְרַת שְׁבוּעַת אֱלֹהִים (ve'al divrat shevu'at Elohim)

a: Do not dig in over a bad matter
t: Do not hold out in a bad matter
p: Do not persist in something that displeases the king, or in a plot against him.
b: "Stand in an evil word" (davar, a word or a matter) may mean persisting in a matter the king dislikes, joining a conspiracy, or simply digging in on a losing point. The first clause is also debated: "Do not rush to walk out of his presence" can mean do not leave his service in anger (compare 10:4), or do not be terrified and run. The Greek joins "do not rush" to the end of 8:2. Either way, the counsel is caution before a ruler who "does whatever he wants".
orig: אַל־תַּעֲמֹד בְּדָבָר רָע ('al ta'amod bedavar ra')

a: "What are you doing?"
p: The same question that Job and Isaiah say no one can put to God. Here it is said of a human king.
b: Job says of God: "Who will ask him, 'What are you doing?'" (Job 9:12; compare Isaiah 45:9; Daniel 4:35). Qohelet uses the words of an earthly king, whose word "is in command" (shilton, an Aramaic-flavored word for authority, also in 8:8). Readers have heard both levels: the courtier's caution before a human ruler, and the deeper fact that no one can call God to account (7:13; 8:17). The Wisdom of Solomon later says the same of God (Wisdom of Solomon 12:12).
r: Job 9:12; Isaiah 45:9; Daniel 4:35; Wisdom of Solomon 12:12; Romans 9:20

a: there is a time and a judgment
p: 'Et umishpat can mean the right time and procedure, or the time of judgment. It echoes 3:1 and 3:17.
b: Mishpat is justice or judgment, and also the right way of doing something. "A time and a judgment" may mean the right moment and the right way to act before a king (most modern versions), or a time of judgment that the wise man knows is coming (the Greek, "a time of judgment", and many older readers). The phrase repeats in 8:6, and it recalls 3:1 ("every matter ... has its time") and 3:17 ("God will judge the righteous and the wicked, for every matter has its time"). The Plain keeps "judgment" so both senses can be heard.

a: No human being is master of the wind
t: The wind, or the breath of life?
p: Ruach is wind, breath and spirit. Here it may be the wind no one can hold, or the breath no one can keep at death.
b: Ruach can mean wind, breath or spirit. (1) "Wind": no one can shut up the wind, a common picture of the impossible (Proverbs 27:16; Proverbs 30:4); the Plain keeps "wind" because the image comes first. (2) "Breath" or "spirit": no one can hold back his life-breath on the day of death, the reading of the KJV ("no man that hath power over the spirit to retain the spirit"), of the Targum, and of many modern scholars, since the next clause speaks of death. Qohelet's other uses of ruach for the life-breath are in 3:19–21 and 12:7, where the notes discuss what happens to it at death.
orig: שַׁלִּיט בָּרוּחַ לִכְלוֹא אֶת־הָרוּחַ (shallit baruach likhlo' 'et-haruach)

a: There is no sending home in battle
p: Israel's law let some men go home before a battle (Deuteronomy 20:5–8). From death's war there is no release.
b: Mishlachat is a "sending away", a release or discharge. Israel's law sent home the man with a new house, a new vineyard or a new bride, and the fearful (Deuteronomy 20:5–8). Persian kings were known for refusing such requests: Herodotus tells how Darius, asked by a father to leave one of his three sons at home, had all three killed (Histories 4.84), and how Xerxes punished Pythius for the same request (7.38–39). Qohelet's readers knew what it meant to be conscripted. Death, he says, is a war with no exemptions.

a: to his harm
p: The ruler may harm the one he rules, or bring harm on himself.
b: The Hebrew lera' lo, "for evil to him", does not say whose harm. Most read it of the ruled: one person lords it over another to that person's hurt (compare 4:1). Others read it of the ruler, whose power ends up harming him, which leads into 8:10: the wicked who held power end in the grave. The Plain keeps the ambiguity.

a: And then I saw wicked people buried
p: The Hebrew is hard in almost every word. Who came and went, and who was forgotten?
b: Word for word: "and so I saw wicked ones buried, and they came, and from a holy place they went, and they were forgotten in the city who had done right (or: where they had done so)." Readers divide it in two main ways. (1) The wicked were given an honorable burial; they used to come and go from the holy place (the Temple); and in the city they were praised, or those who had acted rightly were forgotten. (2) The wicked were buried and forgotten in the city where they had done such things, which would be justice, not vapor, unless the vapor is that they lived well first. The words ken 'asu can mean "they did so" or "they did right" (ken means "honest" in Genesis 42:11). See the variant on "forgotten".
orig: וּבְכֵן רָאִיתִי רְשָׁעִים קְבֻרִים וָבָאוּ (uvekhen ra'iti resha'im qevurim vava'u)

a: the holy place
p: Most take it as the Temple; some as a burial ground; the Targum as the dwelling of the righteous.
b: "A holy place" (meqom qadosh) is most often the Temple or its court (Leviticus 6:16; Psalm 24:3). The wicked, then, were pious in public. Some scholars think of a cemetery, so that the funeral procession "came and went" from the holy ground. The Targum makes it the place where the righteous dwell, from which the wicked are removed to Gehenna, and Rashi reads it of Titus and the Romans who plundered the Temple and boasted in their city (following Talmud, Gittin 56b).

a: the ruling
p: Pitgam, 'ruling, sentence', is a loanword from Persian, one of two in the book.
b: Pitgam comes from Old Persian patigama, "message, decree". It appears in Esther 1:20 for the king's decree, and often in the Aramaic of Ezra and Daniel (Ezra 4:17; Ezra 5:7; Daniel 3:16; Daniel 4:17). With pardes, "park" (2:5), it is one of two Persian words in Qohelet that most scholars take as evidence that the book was written in or after the Persian period (see the book introduction). Qohelet's point is simple and timeless: when justice is slow, people feel free to do wrong.

a: Yet I also know that it will be good for those who fear God
p: Verses 12–13 state the traditional belief; 8:14 seems to deny it. Scholars read the tension in several ways.
b: Qohelet says he knows it will go well with God-fearers and badly for the wicked (8:12b–13), and then says the opposite happens (8:14). (1) A quotation: Robert Gordis argued that Qohelet often cites conventional wisdom in order to answer it, and many apply that here: "I also know (what is taught)". (2) A later hand: older critics such as George Barton assigned such pious lines to a later "Hasid" editor who corrected the book. (3) A real tension: Michael Fox holds that Qohelet believes both: God's justice is real, yet he sees it fail, and he will not drop either side. (4) A long view: traditional readers, and the Targum, place the good outcome in the world to come. The phrase "afraid in his presence" repeats so that the God-fearer and the wicked are told apart by one thing.

a: Like a shadow, he will not stretch out his days
p: Shadows lengthen at evening. The wicked will not see their days stretch out like that, or their days are a shadow.
b: The phrase "like a shadow" can go with the verb: the wicked will not lengthen their days the way an evening shadow lengthens (compare Psalm 102:11, "My days are a shadow stretching out at evening"; Psalm 109:23). Or it can go with the days: his days are like a fleeting shadow (6:12). The Greek takes it the second way, "in a shadow". The Targum has his days "fly and pass away like a shadow".

a: There is a vapor that is done on the earth
t: When the righteous get what the wicked deserve
p: The book's sharpest statement of the failure of justice. The Targum answers with the world to come.
b: Here hevel means something like "absurdity": the gap between what should happen and what does (Fox). The righteous get what fits the deeds of the wicked, and the wicked what fits the righteous. The complaint stands beside Job 21:7 and Malachi 3:15 ("those who do wickedness prosper"). The Targum adds a long answer: the suffering of the righteous in this world clears small sins so that their reward will be full in the world to come, and the wicked are paid now for small merits so they will lose their share later. That answer became common in Jewish and Christian thought. Qohelet himself does not give it; he turns at once to joy (8:15).

a: So I spoke in praise of joy
p: Qohelet's answer to injustice is not a theory but a gift: eat, drink, be glad, as God gives the days.
b: This is the fifth of the book's calls to enjoy life (see 5:18). It follows the darkest verse so far (8:14), and some readers find it a counsel of resignation, others the book's real teaching: when you cannot fix the world's justice, receive the days God gives with gladness. The Talmud (Shabbat 30b) set "I spoke in praise of joy" against "about joy, 'What does this accomplish?'" (2:2) and solved it by distinguishing the joy of a commandment from empty mirth; the Targum makes it "the joy of the Law". Jerome could read the book's eating and drinking as pointing to the body and blood of Christ (Commentary on Ecclesiastes on 2:24); Luther read such verses plainly, as praise of the daily gifts of God.

a: to eat and drink and be glad
p: Isaiah's revelers said something like it before, and the rich fool of Jesus' parable says it in the same Greek words.
b: In Isaiah 22:13 the people of Jerusalem feast instead of repenting: "Eat and drink, / for tomorrow we die!" Paul quotes that line (1 Corinthians 15:32) to describe life without resurrection. In Jesus' parable the rich fool tells himself to rest, eat, drink and be glad, and dies that night (Luke 12:19–20). His three verbs (phage, pie, euphrainou) are the three of the Greek of this verse (phagein kai piein kai euphranthenai), so readers of the Greek Bible could hear Qohelet behind the parable. Qohelet's call differs from both: the joy he praises keeps company with toil, and it is received as "the days of his life that God has given him". He is not saying "live for pleasure", but "take your share from God with thanks".
orig: φαγεῖν καὶ πιεῖν καὶ εὐφρανθῆναι (Greek of 8:15); φάγε, πίε, εὐφραίνου (Luke 12:19)

a: a person's eyes see no sleep
p: An odd idiom for sleeplessness. It is not clear whether the sleepless one is Qohelet or anyone who toils.
b: "Seeing sleep with his eyes" is an unusual way to say sleeping; the Hebrew has "his eyes", without saying whose. It may describe Qohelet's own sleepless search, the restless business of the world (compare 2:23, "even at night his heart does not lie down"), or the scholar who studies day and night, as the Targum has it. The Plain marks the clause as an aside, since it interrupts the sentence that runs on into 8:17.
orig: שֵׁנָה בְּעֵינָיו אֵינֶנּוּ רֹאֶה (shenah be'enav 'enennu ro'eh)

a: a human being is not able to find out the work that is done under the sun
t: No one can find it out
p: The section closes as 3:11 did: no one can find out the work of God. Job and Paul say the same.
b: "Find out" (matsa') appears three times in this verse, and its failure closes the section. In 3:11 Qohelet said God put "forever" in human hearts, "yet no human can find out the work God has done, from the beginning to the end." Zophar asks Job, "Will you get to the bottom of God by searching?" (Job 11:7), and Paul praises God's ways as beyond tracing (Romans 11:33). Qohelet's wise man may claim to know, but he cannot. Addison Wright argued that the second half of the book is built on refrains like this one, "not find out" and "who knows?"
